subject: Unstructured and structured spatiotemporal random effects

messages.author: 4db1b6dd2fb32924
messages.subject: Unstructured and structured spatiotemporal random effects
parts:
Hi everyone,

I want to build a null multispecies, multiseason model, however, some things are still not fully clear to me regarding random intercepts for site or seasons. Would it be redundant / break modeling assumptions to set up an stMsPGOcc() model in which "occ.formula = ~ (1| site) + (1 | year)" and the model includes "ar1 = TRUE" and is using NNGP? If I wanted to set up the model with no occupancy covariates but still allow for occupancy to vary across sites and years is the "ar1 = TRUE" and "NNGP = TRUE" enough? Should I use "occ.formula = ~ 1" instead? Tangentially, for this model formulation if I include random intercepts in the occupancy process, what might the differences be between "occ.formula = ~ (1| site) + (1 | year)" and  "occ.formula = ~ (1| siteyear)" where siteyear is a different value for each site and year combination?

I bring up some of these questions since when running different model combinations, models using random intercepts for site and year along with the structured ar1 and NNGP format seemed to slightly outperform models without the unstructured random intercepts and only the structured spatiotemporal effects when comparing WAIC (though ΔWAIC was about 3-4 which from my understanding means the models aren't much different). It also seems that tMsPGOcc() and stMsPGOcc() don't have any k-fold CV functionality? Is there another recommended method of model comparison other than WAIC for this inference?

Thank you!
Miguel Silva

messages.author: 0b274a0ee3490d75
messages.subject: Re: Unstructured and structured spatiotemporal random effects
parts:
Hi Miguel, 

You should not run models with (1 | site) and NNGP = TRUE, or with (1 | year) and ar1 = TRUE. When you do that, you effectively have two different types of random effects that are trying to explain the same thing (variation across space or variation across time). While in theory they could be estimated given the spatial (NNGP = TRUE) or temporal (ar1 = TRUE) structure, I strongly advise against including multiple forms of site-level effects or multiple forms of temporal random effects in the model at once. In general, using the truly spatial random effects (NNGP = TRUE) to accommodate variation across sites is typically preferred for multiple reasons, particularly if you're doing prediction after fitting the model. Whether using ar1 = TRUE or (1 | year) will largely depend on the size of your data set. With more years, you may see ar1 work better. When you're only working with a handful or so of years, they will likely give very similar results, in which case (1 | year) will likely be favored since it contains one less parameter. 

You are correct that the multi-season multi-species functions do not have k-fold CV functionality built in. The only built-in way in the software to do model comparison for these functions is to use WAIC. However, you can certainly do cross-validation yourself outside of the built-in package infrastructure. This would involve splitting the data set up, running models while holding out part of the data set, predciting at the held out sites, then calculating some comparison metric from the predicted values to compare different model forms. 

Hope that helps,

Jeff

messages.author: 4db1b6dd2fb32924
messages.subject: Re: Unstructured and structured spatiotemporal random effects
parts:
Hi Jeff,

Thank you for clarifying about not mixing up unstructured and structured random effects of similar kind! I suspected as much but wanted to make sure.

I was wondering about the use of NNGP for my data. I only have 60 sites included in each model, which are all spaced on a grid ~1km apart from each other. I think on average, the furthest cameras in my different study locations from each other aren't more than 30km apart. I fit a few different tMsPGOcc and stMsPGOcc models and below are my WAIC values. For the stMsPGOcc, I used n.factors=4, and n.neighbors=5, though not sure how much the models would change by adjusting these parameters.

NON-SPATIAL MODELS:
tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1 & ar1=F: 11926.4878
tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|site) & ar1=F: 11843.7667
tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|year) & ar1=F: 11738.4446
tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1 & ar1=TRUE: 11725.4755
tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|site) +  (1|year) & ar1=F: 11603.475
tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|site) & ar1=TRUE: 11594.7365
SPATIAL MODELS w/ NNGP=TRUE:
stMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1  & ar1=F: 11807.2522
stMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ 1  & ar1=TRUE: 11804.5163
stMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|year) & ar1=F: 11586.645

I know that this is just models ran at one of several locations so may not be fully representative of all my data, but my sense is that one unstructured random effect (either site or year) with one structured random effect (ar1 or NNGP) is likely the way to go. These models had 8 years and 13 species. I feel that  "tMsPGOcc w/ occu ~ (1|site) & ar1=TRUE" may be the model I want since I'm not sure how much the NNGP is improving model estimates (the model with the ar1 and NNGP process together seemed to not be the best performing). I know that there are issues with WAIC not being as reliable with hierarchical models with multiple random effect structures so I'm not sure if there is a more preferable method for selecting a model here? 

I'd be happy to send over any other details that might help with all this as well. I am mainly interested in obtaining the estimated psi values at each camera for the different species, and not really interested in the coefficient responses for this specific work right now. I did run these same models with additional site/year level covariates for the occupancy process and they seemed to lower the WAIC score of each model by 5-10, which has me believe most of the variation is likely not captured by the covariates themselves, and models without covariates could be good for estimating the occupancy values?

Thank you!
Miguel

messages.author: 0b274a0ee3490d75
messages.subject: Re: Unstructured and structured spatiotemporal random effects
parts:
Hi Miguel, 

Based on what you said, I think a standard (1 | site) random effect is likely suitable for your purposes, although it depends on a variety of factors. WAIC is useful, but its not surprising that you see fairly close WAIC values between these different models given the relatively small sample size in terms of locations for spatial models. If your goal is to solely estimate occupancy at the specific camera trap locations for the different species and you aren't doing prediction at unobserved locations, your estimates between the NNGP model and the (1 | site) model will likely be very similar. So, in practice, while one model might have slightly better WAIC than another, your conclusions would likely be effectively identical, in which case the simpler (1 | site) model would preferred. You should also look at the estimated effective spatial range of the estimated spatial factors. If they all are very small, this indicates there is not much information that can be leveraged across space to improve predictions at unobserved locations, which then minimizes the benefits of the NNGP. If the estimated effective spatial ranges are sufficiently large relative to the distribution of sites in your study area, then that is when the NNGP could prove useful in generating predictions of occupancy probability at new sites. Again, if you're not predicting at new sites, the (1 | site) effect will likely be sufficient. There is not necessarily one right approach, but looking at the predicted occupancy values at the camera locations (which seems like your main objective) and comparing those across models may reveal that the extra complexity provided by the NNGP is not necessary. 

Jeff
